subject: Archaeology
title: Roman Aqueducts: Water for Millions
description: A short lesson to help you apply Roman Aqueducts: Water for Millions.

hook.text: Rome's aqueducts delivered 300 million gallons of water daily — more per person than many modern cities provide.

buildup.text: Eleven aqueducts fed Rome, some stretching 60 miles from mountain springs. Water flowed by gravity alone.

discovery.text: The Pont du Gard in France stands 160 feet tall and carried water across a valley for 500 years without pumps.

twist.text: Romans used lead pipes inside cities. Some historians blamed lead poisoning for the empire's decline — but levels were low.

climax.text: Some Roman aqueducts still carry water today. Engineers in the 21st century have not improved on the basic design.

punchline.text: Gravity-fed water with no pumps and no electricity. Still running.

quiz.question: How did Roman aqueducts move water over long distances?
options: Slave-powered pumps pushed water uphill through pipes
Water flowed entirely by gravity from mountain springs
Windmills at relay stations moved water through the system

details.summary: Roman aqueducts delivered hundreds of millions of liters of fresh water daily to cities across the empire using gravity alone. The Pont du Gard in France and the aqueducts of Rome demonstrate engineering that reliably transported water over distances of up to 100 kilometers.
details.whyItMatters: Clean water is the foundation of urban life. Roman aqueducts made million-person cities possible for the first time and set a standard of public water infrastructure not matched again until the 19th century.
takeaways: Aqueducts delivered hundreds of millions of liters daily by gravity
Some carried water over distances exceeding 100 kilometers
They enabled the first million-person cities in history

faq.question: How did Roman aqueducts work without pumps?
faq.answer: They relied entirely on gravity. Engineers surveyed precise gradients — typically dropping just a few centimeters per 100 meters — to maintain steady water flow over vast distances. Most of the channel ran underground in covered conduits; the famous arched bridges were only needed to cross valleys.

faq.question: How many aqueducts served Rome?
faq.answer: Eleven major aqueducts served the city at its peak, delivering an estimated one million cubic meters of water daily — roughly 1,000 liters per person. This volume supported not just drinking but public baths, fountains, latrines, and ornamental displays.
